notes.meaning: Samaria was the proud capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, sitting on a fertile hill like a flower wreath on a drunkard's head. Its leaders lived for luxury and heavy drinking while ignoring God. Their worldly pride is now like a fading flower that will soon wither away.
God is sending a powerful invader, the Assyrian empire, to bring down Israel's pride. Like a sudden hailstorm or a destructive flash flood, this army will smash Samaria's glory to the ground.
The proud crown of the drunkards will be trampled in the dirt under enemy feet. Instead of enjoying royal status and safety, these careless leaders will face total defeat and shame.

Samaria's beauty is compared to an early fig that ripens before the normal summer harvest. As soon as someone spots such a sweet fruit, they pluck it and swallow it right away. In the same manner, the king of Assyria will swiftly devour the northern kingdom.

When human pride is stripped away, the Lord Himself will become the true crown of glory for the surviving remnant of His people. The faithful will find lasting beauty and joy in God rather than in worldly wealth.
The Lord will give wisdom and fairness to judges so they make honest decisions in court. He will also grant courage and strength to soldiers defending the city gates against enemy attacks.

Isaiah turns his warning to the southern kingdom of Judah, showing that its leaders are just as guilty. Even the priests and prophets are staggering from wine and strong drink while performing sacred duties. Because their minds are clouded, they give false visions and make ruined legal rulings.
The prophet describes the banquet tables of these religious leaders covered in filthy vomit. Their drunken gatherings show how deeply they have fallen into moral and spiritual decay.

The drunken leaders scoff at Isaiah and complain about his preaching. They ask whether he thinks they are tiny babies who have just stopped nursing. They resent being spoken to as if they were toddlers who know nothing.
The mockers make fun of Isaiah's teaching style by mimicking his short, repetitive words. They view God's instructions as annoying, childish rules repeated line by line and bit by bit.
Because the people sneered at God's gentle instruction, God will speak to them through foreign invaders. They will hear the strange, harsh speech of the Assyrian conquerors marching into their land.
God had offered His people peace, refreshing, and true rest if they would only trust and obey Him. Yet the leaders stubbornly refused to listen to His gracious promises.
Because they mocked God's clear messages, His words will become the very trap that trips them up. They will stagger backward, fall, and be snared and captured by their enemies.
The prophet directly confronts the arrogant rulers in Jerusalem who laugh at God's warnings. They thought their worldly schemes made them far too clever to be judged.
These rulers boast that they have made a deal with death and the grave so that disaster cannot harm them. They put their trust in dishonest political alliances and deceit rather than relying on God.

The Lord reveals the only real security by placing a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion. Anyone who trusts in this firm foundation will never panic or be shaken. Christian teaching recognizes this foundation stone as Jesus Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the cornerstone originally pointed to God's presence and the temple in Jerusalem, while prefiguring the Messiah.

notes.meaning: God will use justice and righteousness as His measuring line and plumb line to test every structure. A storm of hail and rising floodwaters will sweep away the leaders' refuge of lies and expose their false security.
The leaders' imagined treaty with death will be completely cancelled and erased. When the crushing enemy army marches through like a flood, the scoffers will be trampled beneath it.
The invading army will sweep across the land again and again, day and night, without giving any relief. Just hearing the terrifying news of its approach will bring sheer dread to the people.
A common proverb shows how useless their political schemes will be. Their plans are like a bed too short to stretch out on, with a blanket too narrow to keep a person warm.

In past times, God fought miraculously at Mount Perazim and Gibeon to defend His people from their enemies. Now He will rise up against His own rebellious people, an act of judgment so contrary to His normal blessing that it is called His strange work.
The leaders are warned to stop mocking God, or the chains of their captivity will only become tighter and heavier. The Lord has already issued an unavoidable decree of destruction against the land.
Isaiah calls for deep silence and careful attention as he prepares to tell a teaching story. He invites his listeners to discover how God works by looking at the wisdom of a farmer.
A farmer does not spend all his time plowing and breaking up the dirt. Plowing is only a temporary stage meant to prepare the ground for the seed.

Once the ground is level, the farmer sows each seed with care according to its nature. Delicate spices like caraway and cumin are scattered gently, while grains like wheat and barley are planted in neat, proper rows.
The farmer understands the right seasons and methods because God Himself instructs him with common sense. Human skill in cultivating the earth is a gift that comes from the Creator.
A farmer also uses good judgment when harvesting his crops. Delicate seeds like caraway and cumin are beaten gently with a light stick, never crushed under heavy cartwheels or iron-toothed sledges.
Bread grain needs firmer threshing, but the farmer does not crush it endlessly. The heavy wheels stop as soon as the good grain is separated from the useless husks.

All this farming wisdom comes from the Lord of Hosts, who is wonderful in His plans and perfect in His wisdom. God disciplines His people with the same careful measure, acting only to purify them rather than destroy them.
